TROPHIC DYNAMICS AND ENERGY TRANSFER

ENVIRONMENTSSC CGL Tier-I study noteRevision-friendly

§ 3ENERGY FLOW IN ECOSYSTEM

  • Energy is the fundamental driving force behind all biological and metabolic processes. Energy flow in an ecosystem is unidirectional i.e. from producers to top consumers.
  • Trophic level interactions help illustrate how organisms are interconnected via food and energy transfer.

TROPHIC LEVEL INTERACTION

  • Trophe means nourishment
  • A trophic level refers to an organism's position in the food chain.
  • Energy flows only from lower to higher trophic levels.
  • At each level, energy is lost as heat, reducing available energy at higher trophic levels.

Trophic Levels

LevelTypeDescription
IAutotrophsGreen plants (Producers)
IIHeterotrophsHerbivore (Primary consumers)
IIIHeterotrophsCarnivores (Secondary Consumers)
IVHeterotrophsCarnivores (Tertiary Consumers)
VHeterotrophsTop carnivores (Quaternary consumers)

§ 4FOOD CHAIN

  • A food chain is a linear sequence of organisms where each is eaten by the next member in the chain.
  • Plants convert solar energy into chemical energy through photosynthesis.
  • It demonstrates the flow of energy and nutrients.

Food Chain:

Producers (plants) → Primary Consumers (herbivores) → Secondary Consumers (carnivores) → Tertiary Consumers

Types of Food Chains

1. Grazing Food Chain:

  • Starts with green plants (producers) that are consumed by herbivores and subsequently by carnivores.
  • Main source of energy - Plant biomass
  • Example: Grass → Grasshopper → Frog → Snake → Hawk

2. Detritus Food Chain:

  • Begins with dead organic matter (detritus) consumed by decomposers and detritivores (e.g., beetles, worms).
  • Main source of energy: dead organic matter
  • Microorganisms play a crucial role in breaking down complex organic materials.
  • (Diagram: Dead leaves → Woodlouse → Blackbird)

STAGES OF DECOMPOSITION

  • Fragmentation: Breakdown of dead organic matter into smaller pieces (e.g., by beetles, worms).
  • Leaching: Water-soluble nutrients are washed away.
  • Catabolism: Microbial breakdown of organic compounds into simpler substances.
  • Humification: Formation of humus (a dark-colored, amorphous, colloidal organic substance).
  • Mineralization: Final step—conversion of organic matter into inorganic nutrients.

Favourable Conditions for Decomposition:

  • High temperature
  • High nitrogen content
  • Low lignin and chitin in detritus

§ 5FOOD WEB

  • A food web represents all possible feeding relationships among organisms in an ecosystem, an accumulation of various food chains.
  • More realistic than a food chain, as it depicts the interconnectedness of food pathways.
  • Reflects the complex and non-linear flow of energy and nutrients.

§ 6ECOLOGICAL PYRAMIDS

  • Ecological pyramids are graphical representations of trophic levels in an ecosystem.
  • With each step from the producer to the consumer level, the number, biomass and energy of organisms decrease. Hence the diagrammatic depiction takes a pyramid form.
  • This concept was developed by Charles Elton in 1927.
  • Following are the major three types of Pyramids:

1. Pyramid of Numbers

  • Depicts the number of individuals at each trophic level.
  • Typically upright - can be seen in grassland ecosystems.
  • This pyramid is inverted in a Desert Ecosystem.
  • (Diagram: Snakes → Frogs → Grasshoppers → Grass, Plants)

2. Pyramid of Biomass

  • Shows total dry weight of organisms at each level (g/m²).
  • Usually upright but is inverted in aquatic systems.
  • In 1938, Bodenheimer gave the Pyramid of Biomass on the lines of Elton's Pyramid of Numbers.
  • Aquatic chain: Phytoplankton → Zooplankton → Small Fish → Large Fish

Terrestrial Ecosystem:

  • Foxes, Owls: 100 g/m²
  • Deer, Insects: 2,000 g/m²
  • Shrubs, Plants: 20,000 g/m²

Aquatic ecosystem (inverted):

  • Fish: 50-150 g/m²
  • Zooplankton: 10-50 g/m²
  • Phytoplankton: 1-10 g/m²

3. Pyramid of Energy

  • Illustrates the rate of energy flow through trophic levels.
  • Always upright due to the energy loss at each level in the form of heat.
  • Given by G.E. Hutchinson & Raymond Lindeman (1942).
  • 10% Rule: On average, only about 10% of energy from one trophic level is passed to the next. The rest is lost to metabolism, heat, and waste.

§ 7POLLUTANTS AND TROPHIC LEVEL

  • Non-degradable pollutants (e.g., heavy metals, pesticides) can accumulate in organisms and move through trophic levels. These movements of the pollutants involves two main processes:

Bioaccumulation:

  • Refers to the accumulation of pollutants in a food chain over time.
  • Occurs when an organism absorbs a toxic substance faster than it can excrete it.

Biomagnification:

  • Refers to the increasing concentration of pollutants as they move up the food chain.
  • Top consumers have the highest toxin levels due to accumulation from multiple prey.

Bioremediation: use of Biotechnology to decontaminate an area.
